transcript.text: Indesit washer dryer washes fine but the drying cycle doesn't get warm at all, clothes come out cold and wet after 2 hours. Model is XWDE 96 something.

Thanks for the details on your Indesit washer-dryer. When a drying cycle produces cold, damp clothes after two hours, it usually points to one of three things: restricted airflow (the most common), a failed heating element, or simply too much water left in the clothes because they weren't spun well enough. Before we look at internal parts, let's rule out the simple stuff. Washer-dryers are very sensitive to fluff buildup and load size. If the lint filter or condenser is blocked, the hot air can't circulate, so the drum stays cold and drying fails. Also, a washer-dryer typically dries only about half of what it washes (e.g., 5kg dry for an 8kg wash). If you put a full load in to dry, it will likely come out damp. Please check your lint filter and condenser (if fitted) for blockages, and ensure the clothes were spun properly. Let me know what you find.

Load was about 4kg and it's definitely spun fine. The door glass and drum stay stone cold the whole time, though the fan is running and I can hear water trickling at the back. No smell or tripping or anything like that.

Since the drum and door stay stone cold but the fan runs, the machine is receiving power to tumble but not to heat. This points to a failure in the heating circuit—either the drying heater element has failed electrically, or its safety thermal cut-out (a fuse-like device) has tripped due to overheating. Before we consider replacing parts, let's check if it's just a tripped safety reset, which is common after airflow restrictions:
1. Unplug the machine and remove the rear panel (usually held by screws).
2. Locate the drying heater element (a metal tube or coil near the drum).
3. Look for a small red button on top of it.
4. If it's popped out, push it in firmly until it clicks. If you find and reset that button, plug the machine back in and try a short drying cycle. If it heats up now, the issue was likely a temporary blockage (like fluff) causing overheating; clean the lint filter and condenser thoroughly to prevent recurrence. If the button is already in, or if it pops out again immediately after resetting, the heater element itself has likely failed and will need replacement.

I unplugged it and took the top off. I can see a heater box with wires on it, and a small round button-like part on top. I can't tell if it's popped out or blown, and I'm not sure I've got the right part. What should it look like if it's tripped?

If the thermal cut-out has tripped, the small round button on top will typically be popped out or protruding slightly. If it is still flush with the casing, it may not have tripped or you might be looking at a different component. From what you have described, the most likely cause is heater element. Some programmes (cool air, refresh, delicates or a low-heat option) dry with little or no heat. Was a cool-air or low-heat programme set (and have you changed it), or was it a normal heat programme?

It was a standard cotton dry, timed 120 min, so not a cool or low-heat setting. I also unplugged it mid-dry the day before it stopped heating, to grab a shirt. Still not sure if that button is popped out or not.

A blocked lint filter stops the airflow, and many dryers then cut the heat to stop overheating. Clean the fluff filter in the door opening (heat-pump models often have a second one at the bottom too). Was it full of fluff (and is it clean now), or was it already clean?
I haven't checked the filter yet, I'll go and look. Is that the same thing as the button on top of the heater box, or a separate thing?

They are completely separate components. The lint filter is located in the door frame or at the bottom of the cabinet to catch debris, while the button on the heater box is a thermal safety cut-out that trips if the unit overheats. Behind the flap at the bottom front there's a condenser unit (or a second filter on heat-pump models). Take it out and rinse the fluff off under the tap, then let it drip-dry and refit it. Was it clogged with fluff (and is it clean now), or was it already clean?
I haven't been to look yet, sorry, I'll go and check the filter and the bit behind the bottom flap now. Should I leave the top off in the meantime?

No, you should put the top back on for safety and stability while using the machine. Leaving it off exposes live electrical components and could cause damage or injury if something falls inside. Check the vent hose out of the back: it should be short, without kinks or squashed sections, and clear of fluff all the way to the outside vent. Was it kinked, squashed or blocked (and is it sorted), or was it already clear?
Ok, I'll put the top back on. I haven't checked the vent hose yet, I'll look at that along with the filter and the bottom flap and report back.
Run a normal heat programme again for 10–15 minutes. Is it heating now, or still cold?
I haven't checked the filter or hose yet so I can't run it again just yet. I'll do those first and then try a 10-15 minute programme and let you know.
Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. Is it a vented, condenser, or heat-pump dryer, and when did you last clean the filter(s)?

candidates: Restricted airflow (blocked lint filter or condenser) (high)
Overloaded drum or poor spin before drying (medium)
